title: Jotham: A Steady King and a Corrupt People
summary: Jotham does what is right as his father Uzziah had, but without Uzziah's trespass into the temple. He builds on the temple gate and the wall of Ophel, fortifies Judah's hill country, and subdues the Ammonites, who pay him tribute for three years. He grows strong because he ordered his ways before the LORD, yet the people around him keep acting corruptly.
story: After three kings who started well and ended badly (Joash, Amaziah, Uzziah), Jotham is a quiet relief. The Chronicler gives him no late fall. His short chapter is the calm between Uzziah's disgrace and the disaster of his son Ahaz in the next chapter, who will be one of the worst kings in Judah's history. The one warning note is sounded in verse 2: “the people still behaved corruptly.” A faithful king can build walls and win wars, but he cannot by himself turn a nation's heart. That line prepares the reader for how quickly everything collapses under Ahaz, and for the prophets of this era who spoke to the people as well as to the throne.
historical:
Jotham governed Judah in the mid-eighth century BC, first as regent while his father Uzziah lived in isolation with leprosy (26:21) and then as king. A common reconstruction places his rule at about 750 to 735 BC, with the sixteen years of verse 1 overlapping his father's final years. The parallel is 2 Kings 15:32-38, which adds that in his days the LORD began to send Rezin king of Aram and Pekah king of Israel against Judah (2 Kings 15:37), the threat that would explode in Ahaz's reign.

The prophets Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah all name Jotham among the kings in whose days they spoke (Isaiah 1:1; Hosea 1:1; Micah 1:1). Their oracles give a view of the people's corruption that Chronicles only mentions: injustice in the courts, greed for land, worship without obedience. Assyria was also rising again during these years under Tiglath-pileser III, who took the throne around 745 BC and began to press westward.
cultural:
Jotham's building works were defensive and administrative. The Upper Gate of the temple and the wall on the Ophel, the ridge between the old City of David and the temple mount, strengthened Jerusalem itself. Cities, fortresses, and towers in the hill country and forests guarded routes and farmland, continuing Uzziah's program. In the ancient Near East, such building was one of the marks of a successful king, and Chronicles often treats it as a sign of God's blessing on faithful rulers.

The Ammonite tribute (verse 5) shows what victory meant in practice: not only glory but annual payments in silver and grain. A cor was a large dry measure, perhaps a couple of hundred liters, though estimates vary. Ten thousand cors each of wheat and barley would have been a substantial addition to Judah's food supply. That the payments continued only three years hints that Ammon's submission did not last.
literary: This is one of the shortest royal accounts in Chronicles, and it follows the standard frame: accession formula (verse 1), evaluation (verse 2), deeds (verses 3-5), a theological summary (verse 6), a source citation (verse 7), and the closing notice of death and succession (verses 8-9). The repetition of his age and reign length in verse 8 is unusual and may simply round off the account. Two qualifications in verse 2 do most of the chapter's work. The first, that Jotham did not enter the temple, contrasts him with Uzziah. The second, that the people still behaved corruptly, keeps the reader from thinking that a good king means a good nation. Verse 6 gives the chapter's theology in one line, using the image of a road: Jotham established his ways before God.

outline.t: Jotham's reign and the people's corruption
Building in Jerusalem and throughout Judah
Victory over Ammon and the reason for his strength

doctrines.note: Verse 6 ties Jotham's strength to the ordering of his ways before God. Chronicles does not promise that every faithful person will prosper, but it insists that the strength of Judah's kings was God's gift, not their achievement.

The people's corruption continues under a righteous king. Sin is not only a matter of bad leadership; it is lodged in the hearts of ordinary people, which is why the prophets of this era addressed the whole nation.

words.note: Kun, to establish or make firm. Verse 6 says Jotham established, or ordered, his ways before the LORD. The same verb is used of God establishing David's throne (1 Chronicles 17:12). Jotham's steadiness is the human side of a kingdom God makes firm.

Derekh, road or way, often used for a person's conduct. Scripture regularly pictures life as walking a road; Jotham's ways (verse 6) and his wars and ways (verse 7) describe his whole manner of life before God.

Shachat, to ruin or act corruptly. In verse 2 it describes the people. The same verb is used in Genesis 6:12 of the earth corrupted before the flood. It implies not just misdeeds but a spoiling of what should be whole.

christ: Jotham shows both the value and the limit of a good king. He could keep Judah secure, but he could not stop the people's corruption. The prophets who spoke in his reign looked beyond any king to a day when God would deal with the heart itself. Isaiah, who began his ministry in these years, would soon speak of a child to be born who would sit on David's throne and uphold it with justice and righteousness forever (Isaiah 9:6-7). The New Testament sees that hope fulfilled in Jesus, who does not only rule his people but makes them new. The connection here is thematic: Jotham's reign exposes the need, and the promises of his contemporaries point forward to its answer.

hard.q: Jotham reigned sixteen years here, but 2 Kings 15:30 mentions his twentieth year. How do these fit?
hard.a: The kings of Israel and Judah were dated by counting systems that sometimes overlapped. Jotham began governing while his father was still alive, and his son Ahaz may also have begun ruling before Jotham died. Many historians, following reconstructions of the royal chronology such as Edwin Thiele's, explain the twentieth year as counting from the start of Jotham's regency to a date after Ahaz had effectively taken over, while the sixteen years count his reign in a narrower sense. Other scholars think the numbers reflect different sources or later scribal adjustments. The difference is real, but it arises from the complexity of ancient dating, not from a contradiction about who ruled.

questions: Jotham did right, but the people still behaved corruptly. What can faithful leaders do, and not do, for the people they lead?
Verse 6 says Jotham ordered his ways before the LORD. What would it mean to arrange your ordinary routines and decisions with God in view?
Jotham avoided his father's great sin. What have you learned from the failures of people who came before you?
